summary:
Łódź Voivodeship stands within Poland's national legal framework. The clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention and the treatment received in custody. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Polish courts have shown willingness to intervene on that exposure. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The national legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad. In September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights and called for a recognition framework.

At the sub-national layer, Łódź Voivodeship was one of five voivodeships named in the European Commission's letter of 2 June 2020 to the governors of Lublin, Łódź, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie and Świętokrzyskie, following the adoption of anti-LGBT resolutions by that year. The Supreme Administrative Court of Poland revoked the Łódź Voivodeship resolution on 12 October 2023. As an earlier instance of the same pattern, the Świętokrzyskie voivodeship council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021. By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all Local Government Family Rights Charters in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order, including those applicable in this voivodeship.
tangentialFactors:
The Łódź Voivodeship resolution forms part of a national phenomenon. Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 Polish local governments adopted 'LGBT-free zone'-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area, placing Łódź Voivodeship within a substantial bloc rather than marking it as an isolated case. Polish administrative courts struck the resolutions down as unconstitutional under Article 32, which guarantees equal treatment, and the European Commission linked the release of EU development funds to their repeal.

The repeal process concluded rather than stalled. The last remaining zone, in Łańcut, was abolished in 2025, and by 24 April 2025 the resolutions and the Local Government Family Rights Charters associated with them had all been withdrawn or invalidated by court order across Poland.

The resolutions themselves were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal in effect. They created no new penalties and barred no one physically, but they signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate. A visitor to the voivodeship is therefore no longer facing a resolution in force, while the bureaucratic and educational culture those resolutions oriented may outlast the texts themselves.

The protection machinery arriving alongside the repeal runs at the national level and does not depend on voivodeship policy: the announced hate-speech amendments, the postponed Penal Code changes, and the Prosecutor General's special response team all operate through central institutions. Placement decisions in detention, by contrast, remain individual and unstandardised, so the practical exposure a trans visitor encounters in this voivodeship can differ sharply from the national reform trajectory.
localsOnly:
For residents of Łódź Voivodeship, the anti-LGBT resolution adopted by mid-2020 has been struck down: the Supreme Administrative Court of Poland revoked it on 12 October 2023, and by 24 April 2025 every such resolution and Local Government Family Rights Charter in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order. Świętokrzyskie voivodeship had already revoked its own on 22 September 2021, which indicates the courts and not only central government drove the removals.

The constitutional basis for the removals is Article 32, guaranteeing equal treatment. Administrative courts applied that provision to invalidate the resolutions, and the European Commission's letters of 2 June 2020 to the five voivodeship governors, including the governor of Łódź Voivodeship, tied the outcome to the release of EU development funds. The repeal is therefore a matter of constitutional and administrative law rather than a discretionary policy reversal.

The resolutions carried no criminal penalties and imposed no physical restriction, so residents facing police or court proceedings under them held no charge that had been created by the text. What the resolutions did was direct the behaviour of local bureaucracies and schools toward a particular view of which families and identities were legitimate. Residents interacting with municipal offices, schools, and local services may encounter that institutional residue even though the resolution is void.

Recognition of same-sex relationships remains incomplete at the national level for residents as well as visitors. The June 2024 revocation of the directive blocking recognition of foreign marriage certificates removed one obstruction, and the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment describes the absence of partnership recognition as leaving couples in an illegal vacuum, but no recognition framework has been reported as in force. Residents who need legal certainty around cohabitation, inheritance, or hospital access should treat the judgment as a finding rather than as a working regime.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the Polish hate-speech bills at the time of travel is unresolved. A March draft Penal Code amendment clearing the Government Legislation Centre in May was followed by a postponement of approval and by a second bill in late October 2024, and the sources do not state whether either was enacted. The announced law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation is reported as an announcement by the Deputy Justice Minister, not as verified statutory text.

The sources do not state the reasoning by which the Supreme Administrative Court revoked the Łódź Voivodeship resolution on 12 October 2023. The general pattern of invalidation under Article 32 and the linkage to EU funding are documented for Polish local resolutions broadly, but the specific grounds of this court's ruling in this voivodeship are not sourced here.

No documentation is available of a march ban, an organised attack, or a refusal of public assembly in Łódź Voivodeship itself. The inventory establishes the resolution's existence and its revocation, and it records the resolutions' institutional signalling toward local bureaucracies and schools, but it does not evidence any enforcement event in this voivodeship comparable to those recorded elsewhere in Poland.

The treatment of trans visitors in the guarded centres for foreign nationals rests on a single publicised case reported by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, which concerned a Vietnamese national. Whether the Border Guard commander's intervention produced a general practice of supplying hormone therapy in those facilities is not established, and no national audit of the centres' treatment of trans detainees is cited.

Whether Poland's Supreme Administrative Court ruling has any bearing on resolutions still held by smaller municipalities within Łódź Voivodeship at the voivodeship level cannot be confirmed from the sources, which record only the voivodeship-level resolution and the nationwide completion of repeal by 24 April 2025. The relationship between the voivodeship resolution and city-level declarations in the same territory is not separately sourced.
